title: Maryland Matters reporters improve haul in MDDC awards
summary: Maryland Matters reporters Friday brought home eight first place awards, seven second places and two best of show awards Friday from the Maryland-Delaware-DC Press Association for their work in 2025, improving on their haul from last year.
content:
by Steve Crane, Maryland Matters May 9, 2026

by Steve Crane, Maryland Matters May 9, 2026

Maryland Matters reporters brought home eight first place awards, seven second places and two best of show awards Friday from the Maryland-Delaware-DC Press Association for their work in 2025.

The haul was an improvement over last year, which itself was a new high, when the staff landed seven firsts, four seconds and a best of show.

The awards were announced Friday in Annapolis. Maryland Matters competes in MDDC’s Division C, against the Easton Star-Democrat, the Salisbury Daily Times, the Carroll County Times, the Cecil Whig, the Catholic Review, the Baltimore Fishbowl and the Daily State News of Delaware.

Founding editor Josh Kurtz won best of show, recognizing the best work in the state regardless of division, in the editorial category for “What Melissa Hortman means to Maryland.” His commentary on the murder of a Minnesota state legislator and her husband, allegedly by a man upset by her politics, reminded readers that “there are 188 Melissa Hortmans in our state legislature – and countless more serving in local political offices” doing their best despite the commitment and, in these times, the danger.

Christine Condon brought home our second best of show for “‘My world is flipped on its head right now’: AmeriCorps workers devastated by firings.” Her story, about the Maryland Conservation Corps workers who were suddenly out on the street after the Trump administration abruptly shuttered the AmeriCorps program, won in the wild card category, which focuses on a different issue every year. This year’s wild card was stories about how Trump administration policies affected local communities.

Christine also brought home a first in the environmental reporting category in Division C for “Fish fry: Maryland uses electrofishing to glimpse blue catfish invasion.” Christine spent a day on a boat in the Potomac River as researchers used electric pulses to stun and quickly count catfish to get a scope of the invasive species’ spread in Maryland waters.

William J. Ford landed a first place in the breaking news photography category for “Reparations Congratulations,” which captured a spontaneous hug between Dels. Aletheia McCaskill (D-Baltimore County) and Bernice Mireku-North (D-Montgomery) on the House floor after final passage of a bill creating a reparations commission in the state — a bill on which lawmakers later had to override a Gov. Wes Moore (D) veto.

Maryland Matters swept the breaking news photo category, with Danielle J. Brown finishing second for her photo, “No Kings, no fears.” The photo, of a woman holding a small American flag in a crowd of thousands in Baltimore’s Patterson Park, was taken during the first No Kings Day rally last year.

Moore’s veto of the reparations bill earned Christine, Will and Bryan P. Sears a second place award in the breaking news reporting category for their story, “Moore to veto reparations bill, one of a list of measures he will reject.” Moore conceded the veto was controversial, but said another study was not needed. Maryland Matters’ coverage of the veto, its subsequent override by the legislature and commission appointment continues today, as McCaskill was one of only a handful of Democratic incumbents the governor refused to endorse this week.

Bryan won first place in the investigative reporting category for his story on the scant information about the money, and people, behind the NoMoore PAC, a secretive group targeting the governor online with tart criticism. “Federal funding by ‘shadowy’ group trolling Moore leaves questions unanswered” came complete with official Democratic Party complaints to the Federal Election Commission, unsigned emails from the NoMoore group and a PAC office that was little more than a mail drop in a Northern Virginia strip shopping mall.

Bryan also won first in the business reporting category for “Vice chair of House panel says tech tax drove decision to move business to Virginia,” about Del. Brian Crosby (D-St. Mary’s) painful decision to move his company out of the state rather than be subject to a higher tech tax the General Assembly passed that he said would break his Defense IT contracting firm. It was doubly poignant because Crosby, who is not running for reelection this year, was vice chair of Economic Matters Committee and a member of House leadership that pushed the bill.

On a lighter note, Bryan won first for in the feature writing/profile category for “Mineral bill heads toward a ‘chrometastic’ finish,” about David Shore’s yearslong fight to have chromite designated at the official state mineral. The advocate we came to calling “chromite kid” in the office is a young man now: He started his crusade at age 10 and was 18 last year when the bill was finally passed and signed into law.

And, not to be outdone by Will in the photo department, Bryan won first place in the general news photo category for “Sine Done,” which captured Senate Reading Clerk Andrea Jones in a shower of confetti and balloons marking the end of the 2025 General Assembly session.

Dani brought home a second place in the medical/science reporting category for “Thousands of Maryland seniors notified of the end of their Medicare Advantage plans.” Insurers said they were pulling out of the state or cutting back coverage because it was too costly to operate in Maryland, and Dani talked to the plan beneficiaries left scrambling for new, costlier coverage.

Josh won a second place in the state government reporting category for “Get ready for a dizzying debate on energy policy,” an uncannily prescient piece early last year about the coming rumble over utility bills and environmental restrictions. It was on no one’s radar, but turned out to be one of the biggest issues of the 2025 and 2026 legislative sessions.

Christine took second for local government reporting for “A county worker was fired for ‘gross negligence.’ Now, he’s nominated to lead his old agency.” The story looked at the nomination, and later approval, of Samuel Moki to run the Prince George’s County Department of the Environment, a department he was fired from in 2014.

Christine also landed a second place award for her story about changes to a map showing the “environmental justice” impact on certain communities by industries and other polluters. “Maryland redrew an environmental justice map; polluted communities feel left out” focused on residents of Brandywine in Prince George’s County and Curtis Bay in Baltimore County.

Will brought home a second place in the education reporting category for “Child care providers hope enrollment freeze melts,” about the state’s child care scholarship program that was so successful that state officials had to freeze enrollment for fear of running out of money otherwise. That freeze is still in effect a year later.
